content:
You are an expert in neural-network internals who edits model weights directly, by reasoning, without training.

## The model
A torchvision `vit_b_16` image classifier (12 pre-LN encoder blocks, width 768, 12 heads, MLP 768->3072->768,
GELU, class token + 196 patch tokens) fine-tuned on CUB-200-2011 (200 bird species; images resized to 256 and center-cropped to 224). Inputs are normalized with mean=std=0.5.
Its last layer: `heads.head.weight` (200, 768) and `heads.head.bias`, applied to the final-LayerNorm
class-token vector.

## The problem
The model most often confuses class 58 "California_Gull" and class 65 "Western_Gull". On the practice
images: accuracy on these two classes is 43.3% (confusions: {'California_Gull->Western_Gull': 6, 'Western_Gull->California_Gull': 4}),
overall accuracy 84.14%.

## Goal
Edit the weights so that the model classifies "California_Gull" vs "Western_Gull" images better, WITHOUT hurting other classes. You are
scored on held-out images you never see (same distribution as the practice images):
- success = held-out accuracy on images of these two classes goes UP, and held-out overall accuracy over all
  classes drops by at most 0.3 points;
- among successes, a larger gain on the pair is better.

## Tools in the kernel
- `sd`: dict name -> torch.float32 CPU tensor, the ORIGINAL weights (torchvision names, e.g.
  `encoder.layers.encoder_layer_11.mlp.0.weight`, `encoder.ln.weight`, `heads.head.weight`). Read freely; treat as
  read-only (edits only count through save_edit).
- `save_edit(name, tensor)`: replace one tensor of the model with your version (same shape). Saved to disk
  immediately; the latest saved version of each tensor is your submission. `clear_edit(name)` reverts one,
  `clear_edit()` reverts all, `list_edits()` shows them.
- `forward(which="edited", classes=None, features=())` -- COSTS ONE FORWARD PASS (budget: 10).
  Runs the model on the practice images (2875 images, ~14 per
  class), or only on those whose true class is in `classes` (list of class indices). `which` is "edited" (original
  + your saved edits), "original", or "both" (both models on the same images; still one pass). Returns a dict (or
  {"original": ..., "edited": ...} for "both") with numpy arrays: `labels` (N,), `logits` (N, C), `pred` (N,),
  `acc` (float), and, for each requested feature, `feats[f]` (N, 768): f = "head_in" (final-LN class-token vector
  the head reads) or "block{i}" (class-token residual stream after encoder block i, i = 0..11).
- `classes` (list of class names), `pair` = [58, 65], `practice_labels` (numpy, true labels of all practice
  images), and numpy/torch.

## Rules
No gradient descent or training of any kind (no backward passes, autograd, optimizers, iterative fitting of
weights to a loss), and no fitting of weights to the labels by regression (least squares, ridge, logistic
regression) either. You may compute statistics of weights and activations (means, differences, covariances, SVDs,
projections) and design edits from them by reasoning, then check them with forward passes. Edits must be weight
changes (no wrapping the model in new code).

## Answer format
Your final answer: explain what you changed and why, and what you measured on the practice images.

## How to work
- To run code, put exactly ONE ```python ... ``` block in your reply. It runs in a persistent Python kernel
  (variables survive between turns); you get back stdout/stderr (truncated to 6000 characters) and your
  remaining budget. Print only what you need, as summaries; long prints are cut.
- numpy and torch are available in the kernel. Gradient descent and any training are forbidden: no
  .backward(), autograd, torch.optim, optimizers, sklearn, scipy.optimize, or iterative fitting of weights to
  a loss. Code that mentions them is refused unrun. Reading weights, linear algebra (SVD, projections, norms,
  products) and statistics of activations are allowed.
- A code run longer than 1800 s is killed and the kernel restarts (your variables are lost).
- You have at most 20 turns. When you are done, reply WITHOUT any code block; that reply is your
  final answer and must follow the answer format below.
The kernel is ready. Begin.

I’ll inspect the pair’s final-layer features and margins, then design a targeted head-weight edit and check its effect on all 200 classes.


```python
import numpy as np
import torch
torch.set_grad_enabled(False)
base = forward(which="original", features=("head_in",))
X = torch.from_numpy(base["feats"]["head_in"]).float()
y = torch.from_numpy(base["labels"]).long()
L = torch.from_numpy(base["logits"]).float()
W = sd["heads.head.weight"]
b = sd["heads.head.bias"]
p, q = pair
ip = y == p
iq = y == q
ig = ip | iq
pred = L.argmax(1)
print("Samples:", len(y), "pair:", int(ip.sum()), int(iq.sum()))
print("Accuracy overall/pair:", float((pred == y).float().mean()), float((pred[ig] == y[ig]).float().mean()))
print("Pair predictions:", [(classes[int(t)], int(((y==t)&(pred==p)).sum()), int(((y==t)&(pred==q)).sum()), int(((y==t)&~((pred==p)|(pred==q))).sum())) for t in pair])
print("Pair rows:", [(int(y[i]), int(pred[i]), round(float(L[i,p]-L[i,q]),2), round(float(L[i,y[i]]-L[i].max()),2)) for i in torch.where(ig)[0]])
print("Head norms:", W.norm(dim=1).quantile(torch.tensor([0.,.5,1.])).tolist(),
      "pair", W[p].norm().item(), W[q].norm().item(), "difference", (W[p]-W[q]).norm().item())
print("Head bias pair:", b[p].item(), b[q].item(), "feature norm", X.norm(dim=1).mean().item())
```
reasoning:
**Evaluating data performance**

I’m considering a zero-sum row edit approach, which might allow a pair's maximum to increase while affecting others. I need to guard against small norms and check them properly. I can standardize by calculating mean differences and adjusting for any redundancy in the original direction. I’m pondering how to estimate leave-one-out pair performance without fitting. Calculating robust centroids and leave-one-out scores looks feasible without training, but I need an accurate measurement.

The problem is broader than pairwise confusion: 6 of the 15 California Gull images are classified as other species. I’ll keep the backbone and the other 198 head rows unchanged, and examine whether conservative, feature-based corrections to the two gull rows can help both issues.

```python
counts = torch.bincount(y, minlength=W.shape[0]).float()
means = torch.zeros_like(W)
means.index_add_(0, y, X)
means /= counts[:, None]
mu = X.mean(0)
R = X - means[y]
C = R.T @ R / (len(y) - len(W))
evals, evecs = torch.linalg.eigh(C)
delta = means[p] - means[q]
d0 = W[p] - W[q]
mid = (means[p] + means[q]) / 2
print("Covariance eigenvalue quantiles:", evals.quantile(torch.tensor([0.,.25,.5,.75,.9,.99,1.])).tolist())
print("Cosine original contrast / mean difference:", torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(d0, delta, dim=0).item())
print("Original mean pair margins:", (L[ip,p]-L[ip,q]).mean().item(), (L[iq,p]-L[iq,q]).mean().item())
print("Closest centroid classes to each pair centroid:")
for k in pair:
    cos = torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(means-mu, (means[k]-mu)[None,:], dim=1)
    ids = cos.topk(9).indices
    print(classes[k], [(classes[j], round(float(cos[j]),3)) for j in ids])

# Fixed covariance metrics: raw features and two degrees of shrinkage.
metrics = {"raw": torch.ones_like(evals),
           "moderate": 1 / (evals + evals.mean()),
           "strong_shrink": 1 / (evals + 4*evals.mean())}
def metric_apply(v, scale):
    return ((v @ evecs) * scale) @ evecs.T

dirs = {}
for name, scale in metrics.items():
    d = metric_apply(delta, scale)
    # Match the original contrast's within-class variability.
    s = torch.sqrt((d0 @ C @ d0) / (d @ C @ d))
    d = d * s
    dirs[name] = d
    margin = (X[ig]-mid) @ d
    loo = []
    for i in torch.where(ig)[0]:
        a, z = means[p].clone(), means[q].clone()
        if y[i] == p:
            a = (counts[p]*a-X[i])/(counts[p]-1)
        else:
            z = (counts[q]*z-X[i])/(counts[q]-1)
        di = metric_apply(a-z, scale)*s
        loo.append((X[i]-(a+z)/2) @ di)
    loo = torch.stack(loo)
    correct = (loo > 0) == (y[ig] == p)
    print(name, "norm", round(d.norm().item(),3),
          "cos original", round(torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(d,d0,dim=0).item(),3),
          "in-sample pairwise", int((((margin>0)==(y[ig]==p))).sum()),
          "leave-one-out pairwise", int(correct.sum()),
          "by class", int(correct[:15].sum()), int(correct[15:].sum()),
          "LOO signed margin mean", round(float((loo*torch.where(y[ig]==p,1.,-1.)).mean()),3))
```

**Analyzing feature performance**

I'm considering how the full general pair mean direction can train models effectively, but LOOCV will help reveal insights. I think I need to include pair common boosts and use the centroid blend technique for recovery. Also, computing the global covariance from various features across labels could improve outcomes.

Regularization of covariance in LDA might enhance performance, and blending with prototype deltas seems promising. I want to maximize held-out improvements while analyzing performance under cosine means and maintaining scaling norms. It sounds like there's a lot of potential here!**Optimizing weight fitting**

I'm exploring how to avoid exhaustive searches when fitting weights to loss by using fixed candidates. I can evaluate a small number of options instead of creating a massive parameter grid. I'll test both raw and modestly whitened directions through cross-validation. 

Since I have a small sample size, I'll keep leave-one-out approaches to enhance statistical reliability. It might also be useful to inspect feature statistics using SVD to analyze covariances. Whitening will help emphasize distinguishing features that aren't currently represented well.

The centroid directions show only a modest leave-one-out improvement, so replacing the learned classifier outright looks risky. I’ll test blends with the existing contrast and small shared boosts to the two gull logits, using the cached features to check every practice image.

```python

print("Other gull baselines:", [(k,classes[k],int(counts[k]),int(((pred==y)&(y==k)).sum())) for k in range(58,66)])

# Leave-one-out centroid contrasts, with a fixed covariance metric.
loo_margins = {}
full_margins = {}
for name, scale in metrics.items():
    d = dirs[name]
    rawd = metric_apply(delta, scale)
    s = d.norm()/rawd.norm()
    full_margins[name] = (X-mid) @ d
    vals=[]
    for i in pairidx:
        a,z = means[p].clone(), means[q].clone()
        if y[i] == p: a=(counts[p]*a-X[i])/(counts[p]-1)
        else: z=(counts[q]*z-X[i])/(counts[q]-1)
        vals.append((X[i]-(a+z)/2) @ (metric_apply(a-z,scale)*s))
    loo_margins[name] = torch.stack(vals)

def assess_logits(logits, pair_loo=None):
    pr = logits.argmax(1)
    pc = int((pr[ig]==y[ig]).sum())
    nc = int((pr[~ig]==y[~ig]).sum())
    out = {"pair":pc, "other_delta":nc-int((pred[~ig]==y[~ig]).sum()),
           "overall":round(100*float((pr==y).float().mean()),3)}
    if pair_loo is not None:
        out["LOO_pair"]=int((pair_loo.argmax(1)==y[ig]).sum())
    changed=torch.where((pr!=pred)&~ig)[0]
    out["other_changed"] = len(changed)
    return out

for name,alpha,boost in [
    ("raw",0.,1.), ("raw",0.,2.),
    ("raw",.5,1.), ("strong_shrink",.5,1.),
    ("moderate",.5,1.), ("strong_shrink",1.,1.),
    ("strong_shrink",.5,2.),
]:
    m = (1-alpha)*(origmargin - origmargin[ig].mean()) + alpha*full_margins[name]
    # Equal-prior centering also gets a leave-one-out check.
    center_loo=[]
    for i in pairidx:
        cp=(origmargin[ip].sum()-(origmargin[i] if ip[i] else 0))/(counts[p]-(1 if ip[i] else 0))
        cq=(origmargin[iq].sum()-(origmargin[i] if iq[i] else 0))/(counts[q]-(1 if iq[i] else 0))
        center_loo.append((cp+cq)/2)
    center_loo=torch.stack(center_loo)
    ml=(1-alpha)*(origmargin[ig]-center_loo)+alpha*loo_margins[name]
    ll=L.clone()
    ll[:,p]=pairavg+boost+m/2
    ll[:,q]=pairavg+boost-m/2

    lp[:,p]=pairavg[ig]+boost+ml/2
    lp[:,q]=pairavg[ig]+boost-ml/2
    print(name, "blend",alpha,"boost",boost, assess_logits(ll,lp))
```

```python
    ("gull",Cgull,1.),
    ("gull_strong",Cgull,4.),
    ("gull_global",.5*Cgull+.5*Cnonpair,1.)
]:

    metric_matrices[name] = (U * (1/(ev+shrink*ev.mean()))[None,:]) @ U.T

    return d,full,torch.stack(loo)
```

```python

Cgother = Rgo.T @ Rgo/ngo

def honest_contrast(cov, shrink, local_coeff=0.):
    ev,U=torch.linalg.eigh(cov)
    lam=shrink*ev.mean()
    M=(U*(1/(ev+lam))[None,:])@U.T
    d=M@delta

honest={}
for name,cov,shrink,coeff in [
    ("gull_honest",Cgull,1.,1/ng),
    ("gull_strong_honest",Cgull,4.,1/ng),

    ("other_gulls",Cgother,1.,0.),
    ("other_gulls_strong",Cgother,4.,0.),
```

The strong gull-covariance result did not survive the leakage check, so I won’t rely on it. Next I’ll test lower-variance contrasts that use only broad feature directions supported across classes.


```python
otherclass = torch.tensor([k for k in range(200) if k not in pair])
A = means[otherclass]-means[otherclass].mean(0)
_, sv, V = torch.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
_, sw, Vw = torch.linalg.svd(W[otherclass]-W[otherclass].mean(0), full_matrices=False)
print("Between-class cumulative variance:", [(r, round(float(sv[:r].square().sum()/sv.square().sum()),3)) for r in [16,32,64,128]])
subspaces={}
for name, basis, rank, whiten in [
    ("mean32",V,32,False), ("mean64",V,64,False),
    ("mean128",V,128,False), ("head64",Vw,64,False),
    ("head128",Vw,128,False), ("head198",Vw,198,False),
    ("mean64_white",V,64,True), ("head128_white",Vw,128,True)
]:
    U=basis[:rank].T
    if whiten:
        cr=U.T@Cnonpair@U
        e,Q=torch.linalg.eigh(cr)
        M=U@(Q*(1/(e+e.mean()))[None,:])@Q.T@U.T
```
